notes.11:8: The Greek noun anaideia (rendered "shameless persistence") literally means "shamelessness" or "bold impudence," emphasizing the friend's uninhibited insistence at midnight.
notes.11:17: The concise Greek clause oikos epi oikon piptei literally reads "house falls upon house," depicting either the collapse of one house upon another in a ruined kingdom or a household divided against itself.
notes.11:41: The Greek expression ta enonta ("those things that are within") may refer either to the contents inside the cup and dish or to the inner realities of the heart.
notes.12:5: Greek Gehenna, originally the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, used as the name for the place of final judgment.
notes.12:20: Literally "they demand your soul from you," an impersonal third-person plural idiom equivalent to the passive "your soul is demanded of you."
notes.12:25: Greek helikia can refer either to a person's "span of life" or to physical "stature"; pechys ("cubit," about eighteen inches) is used idiomatically for a small measure.
notes.12:29: Greek meteorizesthe, occurring only here in the New Testament, literally means to be lifted up or tossed about in midair, hence to be held in anxious suspense or troubled in mind.
notes.12:46: Greek apiston can mean either "the unfaithful" (contrasting with the faithful steward of 12:42) or "the unbelievers."
notes.12:49: Literally "and what do I wish if it were already kindled?", a Greek idiom expressing ardent longing.
notes.12:59: Greek lepton, the smallest Jewish copper coin in circulation, worth half a Roman quadrans.
notes.13:9: The Greek employs an intentional break (aposiopesis) after the first condition, leaving the implied positive outcome ("well and good") unspoken.
notes.13:15: The critical Greek text reads the plural "Hypocrites," indicating that Jesus addresses both the synagogue ruler and all who shared his objection.
notes.13:32: The Greek verb translated "reach completion" (teleioumai) conveys both finishing an appointed course and being brought to perfection in His redemptive work.
notes.13:35: Following the critical Greek text, "your house is left to you" omits the word "desolate" added in some later manuscripts.
notes.14:5: The critical Greek text reads "a son or an ox" rather than "a donkey or an ox" found in later manuscripts.
notes.14:24: The Greek shifts to the plural "you" here, widening the master's declaration beyond his single servant to address Jesus' listeners directly.
notes.14:26: In Semitic idiom, "hate" here denotes a decisive contrast of loyalty—loving even one's closest kin and one's own life far less than Christ.
notes.14:34: The Greek verb translated "loses its savor" (moraino) literally means "becomes foolish" or "becomes tasteless," connecting ruined salt with spiritual folly.
notes.15:8: A drachma was a Greek silver coin roughly equivalent to a laborer's daily wage.
notes.15:16: The critical Greek text reads simply "to be filled with the carob pods," without the later manuscript expansion "to fill his stomach."
notes.15:21: The critical Greek text ends the son's speech here, omitting the additional request "make me like one of your hired laborers" carried over from verse 19 in some later manuscripts.
notes.16:6: Greek "batous" (Hebrew "baths") and "korous" ("kors" in verse 7) are large Hebrew measures: one hundred baths of olive oil equaled roughly eight to nine hundred gallons, and one hundred kors of wheat equaled roughly one thousand bushels.
notes.16:8: Greek "ho kyrios" here refers to the rich master within the parable rather than to Jesus, though a minority of interpreters take it as the Lord's own commentary.
notes.16:9: "Mammon" is an Aramaic term for wealth or worldly possessions; the critical Greek text reads the singular "when it fails" (referring to wealth), whereas some later manuscripts read the plural "when you fail."
notes.16:16: The Greek verb "biazetai" is debated: taken as middle voice it means "presses forcefully into it," while taken as passive it can mean "is strongly urged into it."
notes.16:21: The critical Greek text reads "what fell from the rich man's table," without the word "crumbs" supplied in later manuscripts.
notes.17:11: The Greek phrase 'dia meson' literally means 'through the midst of,' and with two regions named it indicates either the borderland between Samaria and Galilee or a route passing through both.
notes.17:19: The Greek verb 'sesoken' literally means 'has saved,' carrying the dual sense of physical healing and spiritual salvation ('made you whole').
notes.17:21: The Greek phrase 'entos hymon' is debated and may be translated either 'within you' or 'in the midst of you,' pointing to the kingdom's presence among them in Christ.
notes.17:35: The earliest Greek manuscripts omit verse 36 ('Two will be in the field; one will be taken and the other left'), which was later harmonized from Matthew 24:40.
notes.17:37: The Greek word 'aetoi' can mean either 'eagles' or 'vultures'; the proverb signifies that the coming day of judgment will be unmistakable wherever it falls.
notes.18:5: The Greek verb hypopiazō literally means "to strike under the eye" and is used idiomatically here for wearing someone down through relentless persistence.
notes.18:7: The final clause (kai makrothumei ep' autois) is syntactically debated and may be read either concessively ("even though He bears long over them?") or as a second rhetorical question ("and will He delay long over them?").
notes.18:13: The Greek verb hilasthēti carries the liturgical sense of "be propitious" or "show atoning mercy," and the definite article in tō hamartōlō ("the sinner") underscores the tax collector's deep sense of personal guilt.
notes.18:24: Following the Saints Greek Critical Text, this verse reads simply "looking at him, Jesus said," without the additional phrase "seeing that he had become very sorrowful" present in later manuscripts.
notes.18:42: The Greek verb sōzō ("has saved you") holds a purposeful dual sense in Luke, signifying both physical healing ("has made you well") and spiritual salvation.
notes.19:13: A mina was a Greek unit of silver currency equal to one hundred drachmas, roughly three to four months' wages for an ordinary laborer.
notes.19:25: The bystanders' interruption breaks into the nobleman's command in verse 24, and he resumes his reply in verse 26; some ancient manuscripts omit verse 25.
notes.19:38: The Greek places anarthrous "King" (basileus) directly in apposition to the Septuagint citation of Psalm 118:26 ("He who comes in the name of the Lord").
notes.19:46: Following the Greek critical text, the quotation from Isaiah 56:7 omits the future verb "shall be," reading directly as a nominal clause ("My house is a house of prayer").
notes.20:17: The quotation is from Psalm 118:22 (LXX 117:22); "head of the corner" renders the Greek idiom for the principal cornerstone or keystone of a building.
notes.20:23: The critical Greek text omits the question "Why do you test Me?" found in some later manuscripts.
notes.20:30: In the critical Greek text this verse consists solely of "and the second," sharing the verb "took her" with verse thirty-one; later manuscripts supply a fuller clause here.
notes.20:37: The Greek phrase "at the bush" refers to the scriptural passage about the burning bush (Exodus 3:6), where God reveals His name to Moses.
notes.21:2: Greek lepta, the smallest Jewish copper coins, worth only a tiny fraction of a day's wage.
notes.21:19: The Greek text reads the aorist imperative ktesasthe ("gain possession of"), whereas several manuscripts read the future indicative ktesesthe ("you will gain"); Greek psychas can denote either "souls" or "lives."
notes.21:25: The Greek text reads the genitive noun echous ("at the roaring of the sea and the surging waves"), whereas later manuscripts read the feminine participle echouses ("the sea and the waves roaring").
notes.21:36: The Greek text reads katischysete ("may have strength" or "prevail"), whereas other manuscripts read kataxiothete ("may be counted worthy").
notes.22:20: While Codex Bezae and several Old Latin manuscripts omit 22:19b-20 (resulting in a shorter text with only the cup of v. 17), the longer text is supported by the earliest papyrus (P75) and nearly all Greek manuscripts. In Greek, the participle "which is poured out" is neuter, agreeing grammatically with "cup" as metonymy for the blood within it.
notes.22:29: The verb translated "confer" (diatithemai) carries the sense of appointing or bestowing by covenant, echoing "covenant" (diatheke) in verse 20.
notes.22:31: The critical text omits "And the Lord said" (found in later manuscripts), continuing Jesus' speech directly from verse 30. Note also that "you" in verse 31 is plural (addressing all the disciples), whereas "you" in verse 32 shifts to the singular (addressing Simon Peter).
notes.22:36: The Greek phrase literally reads "the one who does not have" without stating an object; it may refer back to having no purse or money, or anticipate having no sword.
notes.22:43: Verses 43-44 are omitted in several early manuscripts (including P75, Codex Vaticanus, and a correction of Codex Sinaiticus), but are present in the original hand of Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Bezae, and early patristic citations.
notes.22:51: The Greek phrase literally means "Allow up to this"; it may be addressed either to the disciples to halt further violence ("No more of this") or to His captors to permit Him to heal the wounded servant.
notes.22:68: The critical text omits "Me or let Me go" (found in later Byzantine manuscripts), ending simply with "you will certainly not answer."
notes.22:70: The Greek reply "You yourselves say that I am" affirms the statement while placing the responsibility for the wording on the questioners themselves.
notes.23:16: Many later manuscripts add a verse 17 here explaining Pilate's custom of releasing a prisoner at the feast, which is absent from the earliest manuscripts and from this Greek text.
notes.23:33: Greek Κρανίον literally means "The Skull"; the traditional English name "Calvary" derives from the Latin Vulgate translation Calvaria.
notes.23:34: Jesus' opening prayer ("Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing") is absent from several early manuscripts (such as P75, Vaticanus, and the original hand of Sinaiticus), though widely attested in other ancient witnesses.
notes.23:42: Literally "in Your kingdom," denoting Jesus' coming in royal authority; a textual variant reads "into Your kingdom."
notes.23:54: Greek ἐπέφωσκεν ("was dawning") refers to the approaching onset of the Sabbath at sunset, when the new day began in Jewish reckoning.
notes.24:12: The Greek idiom 'apelthen pros heauton' means 'departed to his own home' (compare John 20:10). This verse is preserved in the great majority of manuscripts, though omitted by Codex Bezae and several Old Latin witnesses.
notes.24:13: Sixty stadia is approximately seven miles (about eleven kilometers); a few manuscripts read one hundred sixty stadia.
notes.24:42: The earliest Greek manuscripts read simply 'a piece of broiled fish,' whereas later Byzantine manuscripts add 'and some honeycomb.'
notes.24:47: The critical text reads 'repentance for the remission of sins' (rather than 'and remission'), and the masculine nominative plural participle 'beginning from Jerusalem' links the phrase directly to the disciples' commission as witnesses in verse 48.
